_note: 2.1.0 (over 2.0.0, which stays as it is): the slide titles and the speaker notes of the deck 3.1.1 (teach slides included), each slide tied to a concept by its example or its title; 52 slides tied.

slides.title: Lists
slides.say: Welcome to Lists. A list is the first data structure that holds many values and can change. Every concept comes with an idea, an everyday picture, a drawn mechanism, the code and what the run printed. The same examples run on the chapter page. Ask: what in your life is a list?

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: the list as a value, changing and searching, loops and unpacking, names and copies, and random choices with short programs. Each code example sits in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this order. Example: part two holds five. Ask the class: which part looks hardest?

slides.title: Three questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Three questions to carry through the chapter. Which operations change a list, which make a new one? How do names and copies decide who sees a change? What differs in current Python? Example: sort against sorted. Ask the class to guess the first answer now, and check it at the end.

slides.title: Part 1: The list as a value
slides.say: Part one. A list is one value that holds many items in order. Indexes and slices reach them, and strings and tuples share the numbering. Example: the lockers of a gym. Ask the class: why does the first locker carry the number zero?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the list as a value
slides.say: The list as a value. Keep the lockers in mind: they explain indexes, slices and len. A pencil list shows that items keep their order, and beads show that strings and tuples are counted the same way. Ask the class to find the picture that fits a string best.

slides.title: Story: why the first item is number zero
slides.say: Dijkstra wrote EWD831 on 11 August 1982 in Nuenen. His reasons are why Python counts from zero and why the end of a slice is left out. Example: spam[1:3] has two items. Ask the class: which rule would you have chosen for the bounds?

slides.title: Lists and indexes: numbered lockers
slides.say: A list keeps many values in order, and an index is the number of one value. Counting starts at zero. Example: in a row of four lockers the last door is number three. Ask the class: what does spam of minus one return, and why?

slides.title: The list: a row of numbered lockers
slides.say: Read the code top to bottom. The first print shows items zero and three, the second counts from the right end, and len says four. Compare the table with the lockers drawn below. Ask the class: which index would be one too far?

slides.title: Lists of lists, and an index too big
slides.say: A list may hold lists, so you give one index per level. Example: a seating plan with rows and seats, where grid of one and two means row one, seat two. Ask the class: where would you meet a list of lists in your own programs?

slides.title: Lists inside lists, and an index too big
slides.say: The first print reaches the letter e through two indexes. Then item ten of a short list raises an IndexError, which try and except catch so the program carries on. The drawing shows the two levels. Ask the class: what would len of grid return?

slides.title: Slices: a part of a list, as a new list
slides.say: A slice cuts a piece out of a list and gives a new list. Start is included, stop is not. Example: spam one to three holds two items, bat and rat. Ask the class: what do spam colon two and spam two colon return, and how do they fit together?

slides.title: Slices: a part of a list, as a new list
slides.say: Five prints show the slices. The table lists each expression and its result, taken from the run. The last line shows that a full slice is equal to the list but is not the same list. Ask the class: why is that last difference important?

slides.title: Why the stop is left out
slides.say: Dijkstra argued that start included and end excluded is the cleanest rule: the length is stop minus start and neighbouring slices fit. Example: fence posts. Ask the class: why would counting from one make the arithmetic of slices more awkward?

slides.title: Dijkstra's rule, checked in Python
slides.say: The first print takes items two up to five and shows three items. The second checks that two neighbouring slices give back the whole list. The chart compares the three lengths. Ask the class: which lengths would change if the stop were included?

slides.title: Sequences: lists, strings and tuples
slides.say: Lists, strings and tuples are all sequences with the same numbering. A tuple cannot change, a list can. Example: a point on a map is a tuple of two numbers. Ask the class: which of the three sequences can you assign to by index?

slides.title: Sequence types: lists, strings, tuples
slides.say: The same square brackets work on a string, a list and a tuple. The table compares the three types on indexing, slicing, length and change. The last line shows in on a string and on a list. Ask the class: what does list of a string give?

slides.title: Part 2: Changing, combining, searching
slides.say: Part two. Lists change, combine, are searched and ordered. For every operation ask: does it change the list, return a new one, or return None? Example: sort against sorted. Ask the class to guess the answer for append before we look.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: changing a list
slides.say: These pictures separate changing a thing from making a new one. The pencil list and the savings jar are the same object after the change. The remote control explains why methods are called with a dot. Example: spam plus equals. Ask: which picture helps you most?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: add and remove
slides.say: Three pictures for three methods. In a queue only the new person moves. On a shelf all the books after the gap shift. On a guest list the names below the crossed one move up. Example: insert at place one. Ask the class which method moves the most items.

slides.title: Changing a list in place
slides.say: Lists are mutable, so these statements change the very list. Only pop gives something back. Example: a to-do list where you cross out, add and remove tasks. Ask the class: which of the four ways to remove or replace would you use for a task you finished?

slides.title: Working with lists: replace, add, remove
slides.say: The table shows the list after each statement, taken from the run. The first print shows the list after one replacement and two additions. pop takes the last item. Then del and remove take two more out. Ask the class: why does pop return a value?

slides.title: Combining lists: + against +=
slides.say: Plus and star build new lists, while plus equals, star equals and extend change the list you have. Example: a savings jar that you top up. Ask the class: which of these would be seen by another name that points at the same list?

slides.title: Combining lists: + and * against += and extend
slides.say: The first two prints show new lists and leave spam alone. Then spam is changed in place three times. The table lists each step and says whether it made a new list or changed the old one. Ask the class: what does spam hold at the end?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: finding and ordering
slides.say: Searching and ordering. A finger moving down a guest list is a search from the front. Re-arranging the shelf is sort; building a second shelf in the same order would be sorted. The guard explains short-circuiting. Ask the class: which of these returns None?

slides.title: Searching: in, index and count
slides.say: The in operator answers yes or no, index answers where, and count answers how often. Example: a guest list on which Pooka stands twice. Ask the class: why must you guard index with try, and what would you do instead?

slides.title: Searching a list: in, index, count
slides.say: Run the code and compare with the drawing of the list, where the two Pooka cells are highlighted. index gives only the first place. The missing Cat raises a ValueError, which try and except catch. Ask the class: what does count of Cat return?

slides.title: Short-circuiting: stop when the answer is known
slides.say: And and or stop as soon as the answer is known, and they return the operand that decided it. Example: the guard who never reads the second ticket. Ask the class: why does the empty list protect the index in the first print?

slides.title: Short-circuiting: stop as soon as the answer is known
slides.say: The table lists each expression, what it returned and the rule behind it. An empty list is false, so spam of zero is never tried and no IndexError appears. Or gives the first true value. Ask the class: what does 0 and 5 return?

slides.title: Ordering: sort and sorted
slides.say: Sort changes the list and returns None; sorted returns a new list. Example: re-arranging the books on a shelf against building a second shelf beside it. Ask the class: what happens to the list if you write nums equals nums dot sort?

slides.title: Ordering a list: sort and sorted
slides.say: The table shows the list before and after each step. Capital letters come before small letters in the first sorted call, and key equals str dot lower fixes the order. The last print shows None. Ask the class: why does sort return None on purpose?

slides.title: Story: twenty answers in a toy, a few in a list
slides.say: The Magic 8 Ball was patented in 1946 in Cincinnati, and the toy holds twenty answers. The chapter keeps some in a list. Example: adding a fifth answer is one more string. Ask the class: why is data in a list better than an if for each answer?

slides.title: Magic 8 Ball: answers in a list
slides.say: The answers are data in a list, and the logic picks a random index. Example: adding a fifth answer needs one more string and no new code. Ask the class: what would the program do if the list had only one answer?

slides.title: A short program: Magic 8 Ball with a list
slides.say: The seed fixes the three random picks, so each run prints the same answers. The table shows the pick, the index and the answer for each of the three rounds. Check that the index is always inside the list. Ask the class: why is the upper bound len minus one?

slides.title: Part 3: Loops and unpacking
slides.say: Part three. Loops walk a list, unpacking names its items, and comprehensions build new lists. The removal trap is the memorable one. Example: a queue where people leave while you count. Ask the class: why is changing a list during a loop risky?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: counting, showing, asking
slides.say: Three small tools. The turnstile explains why range stops one before its number. The loudspeaker shows that print does not change the value. The reception desk explains why input always gives text. Example: a number typed at a desk. Ask: what does input return?

slides.title: Looping over a list
slides.say: Two ways to walk a list: by position with range of len, or by item and number with enumerate. Example: a turnstile that counts visitors as they pass through one by one. Ask the class: when would you prefer enumerate to range of len?

slides.title: Looping: range(), len() and enumerate
slides.say: The first loop prints a position and an item. The second prints a number starting at one, the item and its length. The table puts both loops side by side. Notice that enumerate needs no indexing. Ask the class: what does enumerate of supplies with start one give first?

slides.title: The removal trap
slides.say: Removing items from the list you loop over skips items, because the next item slides into the gap. Example: sending people home from a queue as you walk along it. Ask the class: why does the loop not even notice the problem?

slides.title: Never remove from the list you loop over
slides.say: The loop starts with four letters and ends with b and d left over. The table replays each pass and shows the list after it. The safe versions are a comprehension that builds a new list, or clear. Ask the class: which one would you pick, and why?

slides.title: Unpacking: names for the items
slides.say: Unpacking gives each item its own name, and a starred name collects the rest. Example: name tags handed out at a door, one for each guest in the order they arrive. Ask the class: what would happen if there were three names for a list of four items?

slides.title: Unpacking: names for the items
slides.say: The first line gives three names to three items. The second uses first and a starred rest. The third swaps two names without a helper variable. The drawing shows which item goes to which name. Ask the class: where does the starred name get its list from?

slides.title: List comprehensions: a list in one line
slides.say: A comprehension is a loop that builds a list, written in one line. Example: a stamping machine that squares every number on the belt. Ask the class: how would you write the squares with a for loop, and which version is shorter?

slides.title: Building a list in one line
slides.say: The first line squares the numbers one to six, the second keeps only the even numbers, and sum adds the squares. The chart plots the six squares from the run. Ask the class: what would you change to get the cubes?

slides.title: input() returns text
slides.say: Input always returns text, even when the user types numbers. Split cuts it into words, and int turns each word into a number. Example: a list of lottery numbers typed in one line. Ask the class: what happens if you forget the int?

slides.title: input() returns text: turn it into a list
slides.say: To let the page run the code, the typed text is written out in the first line. The drawing shows the text, the six words and the six numbers. The last print proves that line is a str. Ask the class: why must the numbers be converted before sum?

slides.title: Part 4: Names and copies
slides.say: Part four, the hardest for beginners. A name is a tag on an object, so two names can reach one list. Aliasing, shallow copy and deep copy answer who else sees my change. Example: two keys for one flat. Ask the class which one they trust.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: names and copies
slides.say: The most important pictures of the chapter. Tags are references; two keys are two names for one list. A shallow copy copies the index card, a deep copy the whole folder. Example: changing an inner list. Ask the class: which copy keeps the original safe?

slides.title: References: two names, one list
slides.say: Assignment copies the name, never the list. Two names can reach one list. Example: two keys cut for one flat, so either key opens the same door. Ask the class: if you change the list through eggs, what will you see through spam?

slides.title: References: two names, one list
slides.say: The drawing shows two name tags on one list. After eggs of one is changed, spam shows the change too. The last line proves it: eggs is spam is True, and the two ids are equal. Ask the class: how would you make a separate list instead?

slides.title: Passing a list to a function
slides.say: A function receives the caller's list itself, not a copy. Example: lending a friend your key instead of a photo of your flat. Whatever they rearrange, you find rearranged. Ask the class: how can a function protect the caller's list from changes?

slides.title: Passing a list to a function
slides.say: The call add_hello of nums returns the same list that it changed. The drawing shows nums and items as two names for one list. The last print shows that nums grew to four items. Ask the class: why is result is nums True?

slides.title: Copies: shallow and deep
slides.say: A shallow copy shares the inner lists, a deep copy shares nothing. Example: a copied index card against a fully photocopied folder of papers. Ask the class: when is a shallow copy enough, and when do you need a deep copy?

slides.title: Copies: shallow and deep
slides.say: Changing an inner item of grid shows through the shallow copy but not through the deep copy. The table reads the numbers from the run. The last lines show the trap: board holds one inner list twice. Ask the class: how would you build the board correctly?

slides.title: Part 5: Random choices and programs
slides.say: Part five. Lists meet chance: choice and shuffle, a fairness test, and four short programs that use only what the chapter taught. Example: a toy eight ball and a falling screen of digits. Ask the class: where does chance appear in your own projects?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: chance
slides.say: Chance as a hat and a deck. Choice does not change the hat; shuffle changes the deck. A fixed seed is like agreeing in advance on the order of the slips, so a result can be repeated. Example: the same three answers on every run. Ask: why fix a seed?

slides.title: Random choices: choice, shuffle, randint
slides.say: Choice picks one item, shuffle reorders the list itself, randint picks a number. The seed makes chance repeat, so a result can be checked. Example: a die thrown again and again with the same seed. Ask the class: why does shuffle return None?

slides.title: Random selection: choice, shuffle, randint
slides.say: The seed is five, so the run is the same every time. choice leaves pets alone, shuffle changes it and returns None, and randint gives one throw of a die. The chart counts six thousand throws. Ask the class: is each face equally likely?

slides.title: Story: a fair shuffle, from pencil to computer
slides.say: Fisher and Yates printed the pencil method in 1938, and Durstenfeld published the computer version in 1964. random.shuffle still works this way. Example: three cards have six orders. Ask the class: how would you test that a shuffle is fair?

slides.title: A fair shuffle, counted six thousand times
slides.say: A shuffle is fair when every order is equally likely. Three cards have six orders. Example: dealing six thousand hands of three cards and counting every order. Ask the class: what size of difference from one thousand would make you suspect a biased shuffle?

slides.title: A fair shuffle, counted six thousand times
slides.say: Deal shuffles the cards and joins them into a word. Counter tallies the six words, and the last print shows how far each count lies from one thousand. The bars show those differences. Ask the class: are the differences small or large, and why?

slides.title: Story: the green rain that was never a code
slides.say: Simon Whiteley designed the glyphs of the film's green rain. His sushi joke of 2017 is disputed, so call it a tale. The chapter imitates the rain with counters. Example: one counter per column. Ask the class: what else could a list of counters animate?

slides.title: A list of counters animates a screen
slides.say: A list of counters holds the state of the whole screen: one number per column, counting down. Example: a row of rain gauges. Ask the class: which line of the program decides that a new stream starts in a column?

slides.title: A short program: the Matrix screensaver
slides.say: Sixteen counters start at zero. A column at zero may start a stream of three digits, with chance one in five. Streams draw digits and count down. The grid below shows what the run printed, with the counters. Ask the class: why is the first row so empty?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: summary and practice
slides.say: Pictures for the closing parts. The summary is a postcard, the practice questions are scales, the practice programs a first tune. The two short programs are a box of answer cards and a row of rain gauges. Ask the class which picture they will remember.

slides.title: Comma Code: a list into a sentence
slides.say: Comma Code turns a list into a sentence. Slices and join solve it without a loop. Example: apples, bananas, and tofu, as you would read a shopping list aloud. Ask the class: which of the four test lists is the trickiest, and why?

slides.title: Practice program: Comma Code
slides.say: Fewer than three items are joined with and. Otherwise all but the last are joined with commas, then and plus the last item are added. The table shows the four test lists and their texts. Ask the class: what does an empty list return?

slides.title: Coin Flip Streaks: measure what intuition guesses
slides.say: A simulation measures what intuition only guesses: how often six equal flips in a row appear among one hundred. Example: guess first, then run. Ask the class to write down a guess in per cent before the run is shown.

slides.title: Practice program: Coin Flip Streaks
slides.say: Each experiment is a list of one hundred random flips, joined into text. Six equal letters in a row make a streak. The chart splits the ten thousand experiments into those with and without a streak. Ask the class: was your guess too low?

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. The message of index changed in 3.14, a starred name collects the rest of an unpacking, and comprehensions and list displays came with later versions. The book leaves these out. Example: first, star rest. Ask the class: which of these would help you most?

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. Operations change a list, return a new one or share it. The table says which. The chart counts the examples of each part. Example: sort against sorted. Ask the class to say the five sentences in their own words, then name one trap.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills and two programs. Predict first, then run on the page. Example: spam of minus one is the last item and spam one to three has two items. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence, and to say which picture of the chapter helped them.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Where to go next. The chapter is free online, the tutorial and the sorting guide are the official sources, and the stories link to the notes of the people involved. Pick one link for the week. Example: Python Tutor draws names and lists. Ask: which link will you open first?
